summary: Defines a new optional IS-IS TLV called CAPABILITY, built from sub-TLVs, that lets a router announce its capabilities within an IS-IS level or the whole routing domain. It was replaced by RFC 7981.

eli5.summary: Each router posts a list of its special skills so neighbors know what it can do. A newer RFC replaced this one.

questions: how do is-is routers advertise capabilities
what is the is-is capability tlv
subtitle: Routers announce what they can do so neighbors know their capabilities.

tldr.problem: When IS-IS routers learn about each other, they lack a standard way to advertise what special capabilities or features each router supports. Applications like traffic engineering need to know what each router can handle.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 4971 defines a new optional IS-IS TLV (Type-Length-Value) called CAPABILITY that carries sub-TLVs describing a router's features. The TLV can flood within a level or across the entire routing domain.
tldr.outcome: Routers can now advertise capabilities like mesh-group membership, point-to-multipoint support, or traffic engineering abilities. This enables applications to automatically discover and use these features without manual configuration. RFC 7981 later replaced this specification.

today: RFC 4971 is a Proposed Standard that was obsoleted by RFC 7981. RFC 7981 updates and extends the CAPABILITY TLV mechanism with additional sub-TLVs and procedures.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
IS-IS is a routing protocol that helps routers learn the network's structure and compute paths. As networks grew more sophisticated, routers needed ways to advertise special capabilities to each other—not just their basic routing role, but advanced features like traffic engineering support or mesh-group membership.

Before this RFC, there was no standard mechanism. RFC 4971 fills that gap by defining a new TLV (a standard way to encode information) called CAPABILITY that lets each router announce what it can do. The TLV carries nested sub-TLVs, each describing a specific capability.
sections.eli5: Routers need to tell each other what special features they support, not just their basic routing role. This RFC defines how they do that using a standard format.

sections.title: The CAPABILITY TLV
sections.content:
The CAPABILITY TLV has a fixed structure: it starts with the TLV type number 242, followed by a length field, a 4-octet Router ID identifying the router that owns the capabilities, and a 1-octet flags field. After that come optional sub-TLVs, each encoding one specific capability.

The flags field contains two important bits. The S bit ("scope") controls whether the TLV floods only within the local IS-IS level or across the entire routing domain. The D bit ("down") is set when the TLV is leaked from level-2 to level-1 to prevent loops.
sections.eli5: The TLV is like a labeled box: it says "from router X" and lists what that router can do. Two flag bits control how far the information spreads.

sections.title: How Routers Use It
sections.content:
A router that generates CAPABILITY TLVs must have a unique Router ID. If a router wants to advertise capabilities with different flooding scopes, it must originate at least two CAPABILITY TLVs—one for local-scope capabilities with the S bit clear, and one for domain-scope capabilities with the S bit set. When the domain-scope TLV leaks from level-2 to level-1, the receiving routers set the D bit.

Routers must not use stale capability information. If a router becomes unreachable via the level at which it advertised a capability, other routers must stop using that capability TLV. This prevents confusion when the network partitions or when a router changes its advertised capabilities.
sections.eli5: Routers need unique names and sometimes send their capabilities twice if they want different parts of the network to know about them. They also stop trusting old capability information if the router stops responding.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility
sections.content:
Not all routers support CAPABILITY TLVs. Routers that do not recognize this TLV simply ignore it and continue processing other TLVs in the routing update (called an LSP). This means the extension can be deployed gradually.

For a capability with domain-wide scope to work, at least one level-1/level-2 router in every IS-IS area must support this TLV, so it can leak the information to other areas.
sections.eli5: Older routers that don't understand this feature just skip it and move on. New routers can work alongside old ones as long as enough modern routers exist to pass information around.

sections.title: Security
sections.content: The CAPABILITY TLV carries additional information in routing updates. If an attacker can snoop or modify routing updates, they can learn about routers' capabilities or cause false capability claims to be advertised. Integrity protection mechanisms like RFC 3567 (cryptographic authentication for IS-IS) or HMAC should be applied if the disclosed capabilities are sensitive or if modification poses a high risk.
sections.eli5: Since these are just capabilities being advertised, attackers could learn what each router can do. If that matters, you need to protect the routing updates, but the RFC doesn't mandate it.
